idiom_name: Fluxor feature store: record state, [ReducerMethod] pure reducers and effects
implementation_notes: Fluxor implements the pattern directly for .NET and Blazor: a feature declares its initial state, [ReducerMethod] methods are pure functions that return new state, actions are records, and components read IStore/IState<T> and dispatch through IDispatcher; Redux.NET offers the same shape for WPF/MAUI. The C# 9+ record with a with-expression is the natural immutable-update primitive (s with { Count = s.Count + 1 }), and System.Collections.Immutable covers nested collections that would otherwise be mutated in place. What replaces the classic structure is the framework's dispatcher/reducer pipeline plus record semantics; the classic store is justified when one state is read and written from many components and the transition log matters, while a single screen is usually better served by MVVM (INotifyPropertyChanged or CommunityToolkit.Mvvm) or plain component parameters.
pitfalls: A record containing a mutable List or array is only shallowly immutable: with copies the reference, so mutating that collection changes the previous snapshot too - use ImmutableArray/ImmutableList or copy on write.
Reducers must not perform I/O, dispatch or mutate anything; Fluxor runs them synchronously on the dispatch path, so a blocking reducer stalls every subscriber.
Component-local state hoisted into the global store outlives the component and re-renders every subscriber; keep transient state in the component or in a scoped feature.
An effect that dispatches the action type it also handles creates an infinite loop; guard effect triggers with conditions that the follow-up action cannot satisfy again.
